notes.text: He abruptly tells them; I am Joseph — They knew him only by his Egyptian name, Zaphnath-paaneah, his Hebrew name being lost and forgot in Egypt; but now he teaches them to call him by that, I am Joseph: nay, that they might not suspect it was another of the same name, he explains himself. I am Joseph your brother. This would both humble them yet more for their sin in selling him, and encourage them to hope for kind treatment. This word, at first, startled Joseph's brethren, they started back through fear, or at least stood still astonished: but Joseph called kindly and familiarly to them. Come near, I pray you. Thus, when Christ manifests himself to his people he encourages them to draw near to him with a true heart. Perhaps being about to speak of their selling of him, he would not speak aloud, lest the Egyptians should overhear, and it should make the Hebrews to be yet more an abomination to them; therefore he would have them come near, that he might whisper with them, which, now the tide of his passion was a little over, he was able to do, whereas, at first, he could not but cry out.

He endeavours to sweep their grief for the injuries they had done him, by shewing them, that, whatever they designed, God meant it for good, and had brought much good out of it. See note at "ver. 1" for start of item, ie. No. 1

Be not grieved or angry with yourselves — Sinners must grieve, and be angry with themselves for their sins; yea, though God, by his power, bring good out of them, for that is no thanks to the sinner: but true penitents should be greatly affected with it, when they see God bringing good out of evil. Though we must not with this consideration extenuate our own sins, and so take off the edge of our repentance; yet it may do well thus to extenuate the sins of others, and so take off the edge of our angry resentments. Thus Joseph doth here. His brethren needed not to fear that he would revenge upon them an injury which God's providence had made to turn so much to his advantage, and that of his family. Now he tells them how long the famine was likely to last, five years yet, ver. 6, and what a capacity he was in of being kind to his relations, which is the greatest satisfaction that wealth and power can give to a good man.

See what a favourable colour he puts upon the injury they had done him, God sent me before you — God's Israel is the particular care of God's providence. Joseph reckoned that his advancement was not so much designed to save a whole kingdom of Egyptians, as to preserve a small family of Israelites; for the Lord's portion is his people: whatever goes with others, they shall be secured. How admirable are the projects of Providence! How remote its tendencies! What wheels are there within wheels; and yet all directed by the eyes in the wheels, and the Spirit of the living Creature! See note at "ver. 1" for start of item, ie. No. [1.] [5.] He promises to take care of his father and all his family, during the rest of the years of famine. (1.) He desires that his father might speedily be made glad with the tidings of his life and honour. His brethren must hasten to Canaan, and acquaint Jacob that his son Joseph was Lord of all Egypt - He knew it would be a refreshing oil to his hoary head, and a sovereign cordial to his spirits. He desires them to give themselves, and take with them to their father, all possible satisfaction of the truth of these surprising tidings.

glossa.text: « God sent me, » etc. ((AUG. Quaest. in Gen., tom. III.)) What is it that according to other copies is read thus: « For God sent me before you, that your remnant should remain upon the earth, and that he might nourish up a great seed of your remnant? » For this does not agree in every point, etc., *as far as* « and so all Israel should be saved. »

« Thou shalt dwell in the land of Gessen, » etc. ((HIERON.)) In the Hebrew there stands *Gosen* ( )Migne prints a Hebrew word within these parentheses; our digitized source has lost it and left them empty.. Whence the error grew up that the land of Gessen is in Arabia. Further, as it stands in our codices, it is written with a final *m*, Gessem, which by no means pleases me, as signifying a land rained upon. For Gessem is turned into *rain* , where also in very many copies Gessem is found.

notes.text: Fret not — Because they prosper in their wicked enterprizes.
Commit — All thy cares and business, and necessities, commend to God by fervent prayer.
Judgment — It shall be as visible to men, as the light of the sun, at noon-day.
Rest — Do not repine at his dealings, but quietly submit to his will, and wait for his help.
Fret not — Either against the sinner for his success; or against God. Do evil - If grief arise in thee, take care that it do not transport thee to sin.
The earth — This for the most part was literally fulfilled in that state of the church.
Not be — He shall be dead and gone. Diligently - Industriously seeking him. His place - His place and estate, and glory.

But — Those who patiently bear God's afflicting hand, and meekly pass by injuries. Peace - Partly of outward peace and prosperity, which God in his due time will give them: but principally of inward peace, in the sense of God's favour and the assurance of endless happiness.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* This psalm is as it were the garment of Christ, which covers his whole body with precepts, and protects it from adversities, and cherishes it as in the bosom of counsel. It is a draught against those who murmur at the flowering of the wicked and the toil of the good, as though all things were done by chance, so that, spurning God, they cleave to the world. The Church therefore admonishes that no one imitate the malignant, but that whatever good is hoped for be sought from the Lord, who gives things profitable and eternal.

*The herbs of the grasses.* ((AUG.)) It is now winter, etc., *as far as* because it hath not yet appeared what we shall be.

((AUG., CASS.)) Herbs not of gardens, but of grasses, that is, the meanest, which spring up of themselves through the fields. *Hay,* the noble, who prosper easily; herbs, the middling: but both those quickly wither and these fall away.

*Cease.* ((AUG.)) Anger is sudden, fury lasting; but both are to be forsaken, through which men sin. ((CASS.)) This is said to him who is still weak, etc., *as far as* by doing it he flourishes for a time.
*And yet a little while,* etc. ((AUG.)) After this short life, etc., *as far as* nor did he feel the worm of a gnawing conscience.

notes.text: But some one possibly will say, How are the dead raised up, after their whole frame is dissolved? And with what kind of bodies do they come again, after these are mouldered into dust?

To the inquiry concerning the manner of rising, and the quality of the bodies that rise, the Apostle answers first by a similitude, ver. 36-42, and then plainly and directly, ver. 42, 43. That which thou sowest, is not quickened into new life and verdure, except it die — Undergo a dissolution of its parts, a change analogous to death. Thus St. Paul inverts the objection; as if he had said, Death is so far from hindering life, that it necessarily goes before it.
Thou sowest not the body that shall be — Produced from the seed committed to the ground, but a bare, naked grain, widely different from that which will afterward rise out of the earth.

But God — Not thou, O man, not the grain itself, giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, from the time he distinguished the various Species of beings; and to each of the seeds, not only of the fruits, but animals also, (to which the Apostle rises in the following verse,) its own body; not only peculiar to that species, but proper to that individual, and arising out of the substance of that very grain.

glossa.text: *But some man will say.* Hitherto he has proved the resurrection of the dead by reasons, now he shows by the very nature of things that it can come to pass; as if he should say, by these things it is proved: but nevertheless someone depraved might speak thus, as though the resurrection of the dead could not come to pass by nature: *And if they shall rise: or with what body,* as if he should say: It will not be able to be other than it now is, that is, passible and mortal. The Apostle answers: *Foolish man,* that is, thou who dost not attend to what thou daily seest in the grain.
*Foolish man, thou: that which thou sowest.* So the dead man will be able to live, and in a better body: as that which thou sowest rises better.

*But God gives.* As therefore the bare grain is sown, and by the nod of God rises again in some manner clothed, having many increases with it, so the dead man by the power of God will be able to live, and to rise again in a better body. *To every one of the seeds.* So also for us he will refashion our ancient bodies, as Job says: *Whom I myself shall see, and not another.* But there will be a difference in glory and in dignity, although they be of the same nature. As not all flesh is of the same dignity, though of the same elements, and this is what he says:

notes.text: But I say to you that hear — Hitherto our Lord had spoken only to particular sorts of persons: now he begins speaking to all in general. Matt. v, 44.

To him that smiteth thee on the cheek — Taketh away thy cloak - These seem to be proverbial expressions, to signify an invasion of the tenderest points of honour and property. Offer the other - Forbid not thy coat - That is, rather yield to his repeating the affront or injury, than gratify resentment in righting your self; in any method not becoming Christian love. Matt. v, 39.
Give to every one — Friend or enemy, what thou canst spare, and he really wants: and of him that taketh away thy goods - By borrowing, if he be insolvent, ask them not again. Matt. v, 42.
Matt. vii, 12.

It is greatly observable, our Lord has so little regard for one of the highest instances of natural virtue, namely, the returning love for love, that he does not account it even to deserve thanks. For even sinners, saith he, do the same: men who do not regard God at all. Therefore he may do this, who has not taken one step in Christianity.
Matt. vii, 1.

Into your bosom — Alluding to the mantles the Jews wore, into which a large quantity of corn might be received. With the same measure that ye mete with, it shall be measured to you again - Amazing goodness! So we are permitted even to carve for ourselves! We ourselves are, as it were, to tell God how much mercy he shall show us! And can we be content with less than the very largest measure? Give then to man, what thou designest to receive of God.

glossa.text: *Love your enemies.* When it has been said what they can suffer from enemies, he adds how they ought to bear themselves toward those enemies. And here the Church is not fed with milk, but strengthened with the stronger food of charity. It is not enough not to hate, but what is beyond human nature is commanded, to love. And whereas the law commands a return of vengeance, the Gospel bestows charity for enmities, kindness for hatreds, prayers for curses, patience for persecutors, and even the grace of recompense for those who hunger.

*Pray for them that calumniate you.* That the prophets seem to imprecate, these are not the wishes of men desiring it, but foretellings of things to come: for they themselves prayed for their enemies.

*And to him that striketh thee.* Since charity is patient, it ought to sustain the patient bearing of him that beats; and since it is kind, it ought not to answer curses. If it *seeketh not her own,* it ought not to resist him that plunders; if it *envieth not ((I Cor. XIII))*, it ought not to hate an enemy. *Offer them,* etc. The physician of souls commands those whom he instructs to heal their neighbours to bear all things that can avail for the salvation of their neighbours. And it pertains to mercy that, as from sick and frenzied sons, they should suffer many things, if their health require it, until the infirmity pass. What is so wonderful as to offer the cheek to him that strikes? Nay, every assault of the angry man is broken, wrath is calmed; and through patience he is invited to repentance. *A garment.* What is said of the garment and the coat is to be done also in other things which by any right we call temporally our own. For if this is commanded concerning necessary things, much more is it enjoined to despise superfluous things.

*Ask not again.* Because *charity is patient, is kind ((I Cor. III))*; it not only bears bravely the injuries of an enemy, but also kindly anticipates the favour of a friend, that they may be drawn by other kindnesses.

*And as you would.* Lest he should seem to dissolve the law, he keeps in benefits the return which he neglects in injuries. Nor does he say, as they do, but *as you would that men should do to you, that you also should do to them,* that the return may be the fuller, since the act is matched with the wish. And now extend the works of charity not only to friends, but even to enemies, that they may begin to be friends; and first extend the affection of love, and afterwards the works of charity.

*And if you love.* The more eminent your degree of profession, the more needful it is that the care of virtue be more abundant, that you embrace in the bosom of charity even those who do not love.

There are two kinds of benefit: either when we give kindly what we give, or when we lend to one who will repay.

*But yet,* etc. After he has reproved as unfruitful the love and mutual benefit of sinners, he now shows how these are to be done fruitfully by the faithful, as if he should say: Although such love and mutual benefit profit not sinners, yet do you love, not only by the leading of nature, as they love friends, but by a higher degree of virtue, your enemies. The philosophers divide justice into three parts: one toward God, which is called piety; another toward parents, or the rest of the human race; the third toward the dead, that the due rites of burial be paid to them. But the Lord, having gone beyond the oracle of the law and the summit of prophecy, extended the office of piety even to those who have done hurt.

*Hoping for nothing thereby: and it shall be.* Not fixing the hope of a reward in man. For whether he repay what you have lent, God will nevertheless repay also, at whose bidding you did it; or whether he repay not, your inheritance shall be for ever.

*Be ye therefore merciful,* etc. He rains upon the evil, the earth does not deny its produce, the same sun enlightens the good and the evil.

Mystically: he waters the people of the Jews with prophetic rains, and upon those not deserving it the ray of the eternal sun has shone. If therefore they have believed, be merciful to them, by teaching and by lifting them up, and do not rashly judge, lest anyone conscious of his own offence be compelled to pass sentence upon another.

*Judge not.* There are certain middle and uncertain things, in what mind they are done, because they can be done well and ill. We know not either what he will be like who now appears evil, of whose correction to despair, and to reprove him as though cast off, is rash.

Concerning open things which cannot be done with a good mind, it is permitted us to judge.

*For with the same measure.* It can be taken generally of all things which are done by mind, by hand, by tongue, because God will render according to the works of each.

 *For with the same, ((AMBR.))* God will not repay with an unjust measure, but it is as if he should say: The very rashness of judging and the unjust measure hurts thee, punishes thee, and often not him about whom thou doest this. Or if thou judgest and measurest rightly, it profits thee, it saves thee, even though sometimes not him upon whom thou bestowest these things.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Do not fret because of the wicked; trust in the Lord and do good.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
You meant it for harm; God meant it for good.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
Love your enemies, and do good, expecting nothing in return.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture a brother who was sold, given up for dead, standing now with power over the ones who wronged him.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
And instead of revenge, he weeps and forgives: you meant evil, but God turned it to life.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
This is the hard, holy way: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, give without keeping score.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
Forgive, and you will be forgiven; the measure you give is the measure you will get back.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful!
